lessons.title: Choosing the architecture: augmented LLM → workflow → agent
lessons.summary: The core architect skill: pick the least complex pattern that meets the requirement, and justify the step up in autonomy with evidence.

sections.heading: The ladder of complexity
sections.body:
Anthropic's guidance on building effective agents distinguishes three levels, and the exam rewards choosing the **lowest rung that works**:

- **Augmented LLM** — a single model call enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory. Most "chat over my data" and "extract fields from this document" problems live here.
- **Workflow** — LLM calls orchestrated through **predefined code paths**. The developer decides the steps; the model executes each step. Predictable, testable, cheaper.
- **Agent** — the model **dynamically directs its own process and tool use**, looping until the task is done. Flexible, but less predictable, more expensive and harder to evaluate.

Start with the simplest option, measure, and only add autonomy when the simpler design demonstrably fails.

sections.heading: Workflow patterns you must recognise
sections.body:
- **Prompt chaining** — fixed sequence of steps, each consuming the previous output; add programmatic "gates" between steps. Use when a task decomposes cleanly into fixed subtasks (draft → check → translate).
- **Routing** — classify the input, then send it to a specialised prompt, tool set or model. Use when categories are distinct (billing vs technical vs refund) or to route easy queries to a cheaper model.
- **Parallelization** — *sectioning* (independent subtasks run concurrently) or *voting* (same task run several times for confidence, e.g., multiple safety reviewers).
- **Orchestrator–workers** — a central LLM breaks a task down dynamically and delegates to workers, then synthesises. Use when subtasks can't be predicted in advance.
- **Evaluator–optimizer** — one call generates, another evaluates against criteria and feeds back, looping. Use when clear evaluation criteria exist and iteration measurably helps.

sections.heading: When an agent is justified
sections.body:
Choose an agent when **all** of these hold:

- The path to the solution is **open-ended** — you cannot hard-code the steps.
- The task has a **verifiable outcome** or the environment gives **ground-truth feedback** (tests pass, ticket resolved, query returns rows).
- Errors are **recoverable or contained** — sandboxing, approvals, or reversible actions.
- The **value of the task justifies** higher cost and latency.

If the steps are known, a workflow wins on cost, latency, predictability and auditability.

sections.heading: Exam reasoning pattern
sections.body:
For any design question, ask in order:

- What is the **business outcome** and how is it measured?
- What is the **simplest** pattern meeting the accuracy, latency and risk constraints?
- Where must **deterministic code** (not the model) enforce rules — authz, money movement, compliance?
- Where are the **human checkpoints**?
- How will we **evaluate** it before and after launch?

Distractors usually add autonomy, agents or fine-tuning before the simpler options were tried.

keyPoints: Lowest rung that works: augmented LLM < workflow < agent < multi-agent.
Workflows = predefined code paths; agents = model-directed control flow.
Agents need open-ended paths, verifiable outcomes and contained blast radius.
Business rules that must always hold belong in code, not in prompts.

gotchas.trap: "Use an autonomous agent so it can handle anything" for a task with a fixed 4-step process.
gotchas.correct: Prompt chaining workflow with programmatic gates — cheaper, predictable, testable.

gotchas.trap: Enforcing a refund limit only through the system prompt.
gotchas.correct: Enforce the limit in the tool/backend; the prompt only explains it.

lessons.lab: Take three real requests from your org (e.g., 'summarise support tickets weekly', 'answer HR policy questions', 'fix flaky tests'). For each, write one paragraph choosing augmented LLM / workflow pattern / agent, naming the success metric and the one rule that must be enforced in code.

lessons.title: Multi-agent systems: topologies and when NOT to use them
lessons.summary: Multi-agent designs buy parallelism and context isolation at the price of tokens, latency, coordination failures and debugging difficulty.

sections.heading: Why teams reach for multi-agent
sections.body:
Legitimate reasons:

- **Breadth-first, parallelisable work** — e.g., research across many independent sources, where subagents explore in parallel and return condensed findings.
- **Context isolation** — each subagent gets a clean, focused context window instead of one bloated one; only summaries flow back.
- **Separation of privilege** — a subagent with read-only tools does the risky reading of untrusted content; a different component holds write permissions.
- **Specialisation** — distinct tool sets and instructions per role.

Anthropic's own write-up of its multi-agent research system reports large quality gains on broad research tasks — and also that such systems burn **many times more tokens** than single-agent chat. Cost must be justified by task value.

sections.heading: Topologies
sections.body:
- **Orchestrator–subagents (hub and spoke)** — a lead agent plans, spawns subagents with explicit task descriptions (objective, output format, tools, boundaries), and synthesises. Most common and easiest to reason about.
- **Pipeline / assembly line** — fixed handoffs between specialised agents. Really a workflow with agentic steps.
- **Peer / swarm** — agents message each other freely. Hard to debug, prone to loops and drift; rarely the right exam answer.
- **Evaluator / critic** — an independent instance reviews another's output. Independent review catches errors that self-review rationalises away.

sections.heading: When NOT to use multi-agent
sections.body:
- **Tightly coupled tasks** where every step depends on shared, evolving state (most single-codebase coding changes) — splitting causes conflicting edits and lost context.
- **Low-value, high-volume tasks** where token multiplication destroys unit economics.
- **Latency-critical interactions** (live chat) where serial orchestration adds seconds.
- When a **single agent with better tools or context** would do.

Common failure modes: vague delegation (subagents duplicate work or misread scope), unbounded spawning, lost information in summaries, and no end-to-end trace.

sections.heading: Design controls
sections.body:
- Give each subagent a **precise brief**: goal, scope boundaries, expected output schema, tool list, effort budget.
- Put **hard limits** in code: max subagents, max turns, max spend, timeouts.
- **Trace** every agent with a shared correlation ID.
- Have the orchestrator **verify** results (citations, tests) rather than trust them.
- Keep **write/irreversible actions** out of agents that read untrusted content.

keyPoints: Multi-agent = parallelism + context isolation, paid for in tokens and complexity.
Great for breadth-first research; poor for tightly coupled coding or latency-sensitive chat.
Subagent briefs need objective, output format, tools and boundaries.
Limits (turns, spend, fan-out) are enforced in code.

gotchas.trap: Splitting a single-repo refactor across five parallel coding agents for speed.
gotchas.correct: Single agent (or sequential steps) — the work is tightly coupled; parallel edits conflict.

gotchas.trap: Asking the same agent instance to review its own output as a quality gate.
gotchas.correct: Use an independent reviewer instance/prompt, ideally with fresh context.

lessons.lab: Sketch an orchestrator–subagent design for 'competitive analysis of 12 vendors'. Write the subagent brief template (objective, sources, output JSON, budget) and list the three limits you'd enforce in code. Then explain in two sentences why you would NOT use this topology for 'migrate our monorepo to a new logging library'.

lessons.title: Aligning designs to business value
lessons.summary: Architects must connect every design decision to a measurable outcome, total cost of ownership and risk appetite.

sections.heading: Start from the outcome
sections.body:
Frame every engagement as: **who** benefits, **what metric** moves (handle time, deflection rate, cost per document, cycle time, revenue), the **baseline** today, and the **target**. A design without a baseline cannot prove ROI.

Separate:

- **Quality metrics** — accuracy, groundedness, task success rate.
- **Operational metrics** — p50/p95 latency, availability, cost per task.
- **Business metrics** — the KPI the sponsor actually cares about.

sections.heading: Total cost of ownership
sections.body:
Model tokens are only part of the bill. Include:

- Tokens (input, output, cached, batch) × volume × growth.
- Retrieval infrastructure, vector stores, observability tooling.
- Human review time (HITL is a cost line, often the largest).
- Evaluation and maintenance — prompt/version upkeep, eval set curation.
- Integration and security work, compliance reviews.

Model the **cost per successful outcome**, not cost per call — a cheaper model that fails more often and triggers human rework can be more expensive.

sections.heading: Build vs buy vs configure
sections.body:
Before custom architecture, check whether an existing product fits: Claude apps with connectors and projects, Claude Code, or partner solutions. Architects are judged on **time-to-value and risk**, not on building the most impressive system.

Prefer phased delivery: a **thin vertical slice** to a real user group with measurement, then expand.

keyPoints: Baseline + target metric before design.
Cost per successful outcome beats cost per call.
HITL review time is a real cost line.
Consider configure/buy before build.

gotchas.trap: Choosing the cheapest model per token to maximise ROI.
gotchas.correct: Compare cost per successful task including rework and escalation.

lessons.lab: For one candidate use case, fill in: baseline metric, target, monthly volume, estimated tokens per task for two model tiers, HITL minutes per task, and the resulting cost per successful outcome. Decide which tier wins.

lessons.title: Model selection, routing and cascades
lessons.summary: Match model tier to task difficulty, latency and cost — and use routing so you don't pay top-tier prices for easy traffic.

sections.heading: The tiers
sections.body:
Claude models come in tiers that trade capability for speed and price:

- **Opus** — the most capable tier: complex reasoning, hard coding, long-horizon agentic work, nuanced analysis. Highest cost and latency.
- **Sonnet** — the balanced workhorse: strong reasoning and coding at moderate cost; the default for most production agents.
- **Haiku** — fastest and cheapest: classification, routing, extraction, high-volume simple tasks, sub-agents doing narrow work, real-time UX.

Exact model versions, prices and context limits change — always verify current values in the docs. On the exam, reason from the **relative** trade-offs.

sections.heading: Selection method
sections.body:
- Define the task's quality bar with an **eval set** first.
- Run the eval on the **smallest candidate tier first**; move up only if it fails the bar.
- Weigh **latency** (time-to-first-token, total time), **cost per successful task**, **context needs** and **availability** (which regions/clouds offer the model).
- Re-run the eval whenever you switch versions — never assume a newer or larger model is better on *your* task.

sections.heading: Routing and cascades
sections.body:
- **Routing** — a cheap classifier (often Haiku or even rules) sends each request to the appropriate model/prompt. Most traffic goes to the cheaper tier; hard cases go up.
- **Cascade / escalation** — try the cheaper model first; escalate to a stronger model (or a human) when confidence checks, validation or a verifier fail.
- **Mixed-model agents** — a stronger orchestrator with cheaper subagents for narrow tasks.

Routing needs its own eval: a misrouted hard query answered badly by the small model is a quality incident.

keyPoints: Opus = capability, Sonnet = balance, Haiku = speed/cost.
Eval the smallest tier first; upgrade on evidence.
Routing/cascades cut cost while preserving quality on hard cases.
Re-evaluate on every model version change.

gotchas.trap: Defaulting every call to the most capable model 'to be safe'.
gotchas.correct: Route by difficulty; reserve the top tier for traffic that needs it.

gotchas.trap: Upgrading to a new model version in production without re-running evals.
gotchas.correct: Treat model change like a code change: regression eval, staged rollout.

lessons.lab: Build a 30-item eval for a classification task. Run it against the smallest and a mid-tier model, record accuracy, p95 latency and cost. Write the one-paragraph decision memo.

lessons.title: System prompts, guardrails and extended thinking
lessons.summary: System prompts set role, rules and format; guardrails make them robust; extended thinking buys reasoning quality for hard problems.

sections.heading: Effective system prompts
sections.body:
A production system prompt typically contains:

- **Role and audience** — who Claude is acting as and for whom.
- **Context** — product facts, policies, what tools exist and when to use them.
- **Rules expressed as principles with reasons** — "Never quote prices from memory because they change weekly; use the pricing tool." Reasons generalise better than long lists of conditionals.
- **Output format** — structure, length, tone; examples where helpful.
- **Escalation behaviour** — what to do when uncertain or out of scope.

Use clear structure (e.g., XML-style tagged sections), put long reference documents before the question, and give examples (few-shot) that are diverse rather than near-duplicates.

sections.heading: Guardrails in layers
sections.body:
Prompts are a **soft** control. Layer them:

- **Input screening** — classify for jailbreaks, injection, out-of-scope topics (a cheap model works well).
- **Prompt-level** — clear refusals/escalation rules, allowed topics, "say you don't know".
- **Tool-level** — least-privilege tools, server-side validation, approval gates.
- **Output screening** — PII detection, policy checks, schema validation, grounding checks.
- **Monitoring** — sample and review conversations; alert on anomalies.

Anything that **must** hold (authorisation, limits, compliance) lives in deterministic code.

sections.heading: Extended thinking
sections.body:
Extended thinking lets Claude reason step-by-step before answering, with a configurable thinking budget. It helps on **complex multi-step reasoning, math, hard coding and planning**; it adds **latency and output-token cost** and is usually unnecessary for simple lookups or classification.

Architect guidance:

- Enable it for hard tasks where evals show a gain; tune the budget.
- Don't use it on latency-critical, simple, high-volume paths.
- Treat thinking content as internal reasoning, not a user-facing artefact or an audit guarantee.

keyPoints: Principles + reasons beat long conditional lists.
Guardrails are layered: input, prompt, tool, output, monitoring.
Hard rules live in code.
Extended thinking = better reasoning for more latency/cost; use where evals show gains.

gotchas.trap: Adding 'IMPORTANT: NEVER do X' in capitals repeatedly to fix a policy violation.
gotchas.correct: Explain the reason, add examples, and enforce X in a tool/output check.

gotchas.trap: Turning on extended thinking for a high-volume intent classifier.
gotchas.correct: Use a small fast model without thinking; validate with evals.

lessons.lab: Rewrite a 40-line 'if the user asks X then Y' system prompt into principles with reasons plus three diverse examples. Compare both versions on a 20-case eval.

lessons.title: Context engineering, prompt caching and Agent Skills
lessons.summary: Context is a finite, expensive resource: curate it, cache the stable prefix, and load specialised knowledge only when needed.

sections.heading: Context engineering
sections.body:
Context engineering is deciding **what tokens the model sees at each step**. More context is not always better: irrelevant material dilutes attention, increases cost and latency, and long agent sessions accumulate stale tool output.

Techniques:

- **Retrieve just-in-time** rather than stuffing everything up front.
- **Compaction** — summarise long histories, keeping decisions, open issues and key facts; drop raw tool dumps.
- **Structured notes / memory** — the agent writes durable notes outside the context window and re-reads them.
- **Subagents** — isolate deep exploration; return condensed results.
- **Trim tool outputs** — return only needed fields, paginate, filter.
- Put critical, persistent instructions in the system prompt, not 50 turns back in the history.

sections.heading: Prompt caching economics
sections.body:
Prompt caching lets you mark a **stable prefix** (system prompt, tool definitions, large documents, few-shot examples) with cache breakpoints. Subsequent requests with an **identical prefix** read it from cache at a **steep discount** and with lower latency; writing the cache costs somewhat more than normal input. The cache has a short default lifetime that is refreshed on use, with a longer-TTL option.

Design rules:

- Order content **stable → variable**: tools, system prompt, documents, then conversation, then the new user turn.
- Any change in the prefix (even a timestamp) **invalidates** everything after it.
- It pays off when the same large prefix is reused many times within the TTL — chatbots with long system prompts, agents with big tool sets, Q&A over one large document.
- It does **not** help one-off requests with unique prompts.

sections.heading: Agent Skills and progressive disclosure
sections.body:
An **Agent Skill** is a folder containing a `SKILL.md` (with a name and description in its frontmatter) plus optional scripts and reference files. Only the short **name and description** sit in context up front; Claude loads the full instructions when the skill is relevant, and reads additional files or runs scripts only as needed. This **progressive disclosure** lets you ship many specialised capabilities without bloating every request.

Use skills for repeatable procedures and organisational know-how (brand guidelines, report formats, data-analysis playbooks). Write descriptions that clearly say **when** the skill applies. Treat third-party skills as code: review them before installing, since they can include executable scripts.

keyPoints: Curate context; more is not better.
Cache stable prefixes; order stable→variable; any prefix change invalidates.
Caching helps repeated large prefixes, not unique one-offs.
Skills: metadata always loaded, body and files on demand.

gotchas.trap: Putting the current timestamp at the top of the system prompt in a cached chatbot.
gotchas.correct: Move volatile values after the cache breakpoint (or into the user turn).

gotchas.trap: Loading every procedure document into the system prompt 'so Claude always knows'.
gotchas.correct: Package procedures as Skills or retrieve them just-in-time.

lessons.lab: Take a chatbot with a long system prompt and tool list. Reorder it stable→variable, add a cache breakpoint, and compare input cost and latency over 50 replayed conversations.

lessons.title: Tool design, tool bloat and least privilege
lessons.summary: Every tool is both a capability and an attack surface. Fewer, well-described, narrowly-scoped tools make agents more accurate and safer.

sections.heading: Tool bloat
sections.body:
Connecting dozens of MCP servers or hundreds of tools causes:

- **Selection errors** — overlapping tools with similar names/descriptions confuse the model.
- **Context cost** — every tool definition consumes tokens on every request.
- **Larger blast radius** — more ways for an injected instruction to cause harm.

Remedies: consolidate overlapping tools into higher-level ones (e.g., one `schedule_meeting` instead of three low-level calendar calls), expose **task-scoped tool sets** per agent or route, load tools on demand, and remove unused tools.

sections.heading: Designing good tools
sections.body:
- **Clear names and descriptions**: what it does, when to use it, when *not* to, what the inputs mean, example values.
- **Strict input schemas** — enums, formats, required fields; validate server-side anyway.
- **Return only what's useful** — concise, relevant fields; human-readable identifiers; pagination.
- **Actionable errors** — structured error messages the model can recover from ("date must be YYYY-MM-DD"), not stack traces or empty strings.
- **Idempotency** for actions that may be retried.

sections.heading: Least privilege
sections.body:
- Grant each agent/tool the **minimum scopes** needed (read-only where possible).
- **Separate read and write** tools; gate writes and irreversible actions behind confirmation or human approval.
- Use **per-user delegated credentials** so the agent can never see more than the requesting user could.
- Never give the model raw secrets; the tool layer holds credentials.
- Sandbox code execution and restrict network egress.

keyPoints: Too many tools hurt accuracy, cost and security.
Consolidate and scope tool sets per task.
Descriptions say when (and when not) to use a tool.
Least privilege, read/write separation, per-user credentials.

gotchas.trap: Fixing wrong tool selection by switching to a bigger model.
gotchas.correct: First fix overlapping tools and vague descriptions; reduce the tool set.

gotchas.trap: Giving the agent a service account with admin scope 'so nothing fails'.
gotchas.correct: Per-user delegated, least-privilege scopes; separate write tools with approvals.

lessons.lab: Audit an agent's tool list. Mark overlaps, rewrite the two vaguest descriptions, split a read/write tool into two, and define which actions require approval.

lessons.title: Authentication, authorization and connection protocols
lessons.summary: Most serious agent incidents are authorization failures. Choose the right protocol and make identity flow end-to-end.

sections.heading: Authorization gaps and the confused deputy
sections.body:
A **confused deputy** occurs when a privileged component (agent, MCP server, service account) is tricked into using *its* authority on behalf of a requester who lacks it. Example: an assistant with a broad service account answers an intern's question using executive-only documents.

Controls:

- **Propagate the end-user identity** to every downstream call and enforce authorization at the data source (document ACLs, row-level security).
- Filter retrieval results by the **user's permissions before** they reach the model.
- Don't let the model decide authorization — code does.
- MCP's authorization model builds on **OAuth 2.1**; servers should validate that tokens were issued **for them** and must not simply pass client tokens through to upstream APIs.

sections.heading: Choosing a connection protocol
sections.body:
- **MCP (Model Context Protocol)** — an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools (actions), resources (data) and prompts, over stdio (local) or HTTP-based transports (remote). Best when a capability should be **reusable across many clients** (Claude apps, Claude Code, custom agents) or provided by a vendor.
- **Direct API / function calling** — define tools inline in your application. Best for app-specific tools tightly coupled to your backend, with the least moving parts.
- **CLI** — agents like Claude Code can call existing command-line tools directly (git, cloud CLIs). Often the simplest integration for developer workflows; govern with permissions.
- **Agent-to-agent** — one agent delegating to another agent owned by a different team or vendor through an agent protocol. Useful across organisational boundaries; adds trust, contract and latency concerns.

Choose by reuse, ownership, security boundary and latency — not by novelty.

sections.heading: Trusting MCP servers
sections.body: Treat third-party MCP servers like third-party code: vet the publisher, pin versions, review requested scopes, run with least privilege, and maintain an **allowlist**. Tool descriptions and outputs from servers are themselves untrusted input that can carry injected instructions.

keyPoints: Confused deputy: broad agent credentials serving narrow-permission users.
Propagate user identity; enforce authz at the source and pre-retrieval.
MCP for reusable cross-client capabilities; direct tools for app-specific logic.
Allowlist and vet MCP servers; their output is untrusted.

gotchas.trap: Telling the model in the system prompt 'only show documents the user is allowed to see'.
gotchas.correct: Filter retrieval by the user's ACLs in code before results reach the model.

gotchas.trap: An MCP server forwarding the client's token straight to a downstream API.
gotchas.correct: Server validates tokens issued for itself and obtains its own downstream credentials.

lessons.lab: Draw the identity flow for 'employee asks assistant about HR cases': user → app → model → tool → HR system. Mark where the user's identity is checked at each hop and where a confused deputy could occur.

lessons.title: RAG pipeline design, latency trade-offs and observability
lessons.summary: Retrieval quality usually determines answer quality. Design chunking, hybrid search, reranking and citations — and instrument everything.

sections.heading: RAG building blocks
sections.body:
- **Ingestion** — parse documents faithfully (tables, headings), attach metadata (source, owner, date, ACLs).
- **Chunking** — chunk on semantic boundaries (sections/paragraphs) with modest overlap; chunk size trades precision vs context.
- **Contextual retrieval** — Anthropic's technique of prepending a short, LLM-generated description of where each chunk sits in its document *before* embedding and indexing, so chunks like "revenue grew 3%" keep their meaning. Combined with hybrid search and reranking it substantially reduces retrieval failures. Prompt caching makes generating this context cheap.
- **Hybrid search** — combine **embeddings** (semantic similarity) with **BM25/keyword** (exact terms, IDs, product codes, error strings).
- **Reranking** — retrieve a wider candidate set, then rerank to the top few most relevant chunks.
- **Generation with citations** — instruct Claude to answer only from provided sources and cite them; Claude's citations capability can return pointers to the exact passages used.

sections.heading: When not to use RAG
sections.body:
If the whole knowledge base fits comfortably in the context window and is reused, **put it in context and cache it** — simpler and often more accurate. RAG earns its complexity with large, changing or permissioned corpora.

Also consider **agentic search** (the model iteratively issues queries/tool calls) for complex multi-hop questions, at higher latency.

sections.heading: Accuracy–latency trade-offs
sections.body:
Every step adds latency: query rewriting, multiple retrievals, reranking, larger models, extended thinking, verification passes. Levers:

- Use a small model for query rewriting/classification.
- Parallelise retrieval calls.
- Stream responses to improve perceived latency.
- Cache stable prefixes.
- Reserve multi-hop agentic retrieval and verification for queries that need it (route by complexity).

State the SLO (e.g., p95 < 5s) and design to it; don't optimise accuracy blindly.

sections.heading: Observability at scale
sections.body:
Instrument every request end-to-end:

- **Traces** spanning user request → retrieval → model calls → tool calls, with correlation IDs (essential for multi-agent).
- Log **prompt/version IDs, model version, retrieved document IDs, token counts (input/output/cached), latency, stop reasons, tool errors**.
- Track quality signals: user feedback, escalations, groundedness scores from sampled LLM-judge evaluation.
- Redact or tokenise PII in logs; apply retention policies.
- Dashboards and alerts on cost per task, error rates, latency SLOs and drift.

keyPoints: Hybrid (embeddings + BM25) + reranking beats either alone.
Contextual retrieval preserves chunk meaning.
Small, stable corpus → long context + caching instead of RAG.
Trace everything with IDs, versions, token counts; redact PII.

gotchas.trap: Answers miss exact product codes, so the team switches to a bigger embedding model.
gotchas.correct: Add keyword/BM25 hybrid search — exact identifiers are a lexical problem.

gotchas.trap: Building a vector pipeline for a 40-page policy handbook used by every query.
gotchas.correct: Put it in the system prompt with prompt caching.

lessons.lab: On a 200-document corpus, compare: embeddings only, hybrid, hybrid + rerank. Measure recall@5 on 30 labelled questions and p95 latency. Write which you'd ship for a 3-second SLO.

lessons.title: Evaluation design: eval sets and graders
lessons.summary: Without evals you cannot select models, ship prompt changes or prove value. Build them before you build the product.

sections.heading: Define success criteria first
sections.body:
Good success criteria are **specific, measurable, achievable and relevant**: "≥95% of extracted invoice totals exactly match ground truth", "≤2% of responses contain unsupported claims", "p95 latency < 4s". Vague goals ("good answers") cannot be tested.

Cover multiple dimensions: task accuracy, groundedness, format compliance, safety/refusal behaviour, tone, latency, cost.

sections.heading: Building the eval set
sections.body:
- Draw from **real production-like inputs**, including messy, ambiguous and adversarial cases.
- Include **edge cases** and known past failures (every incident becomes a test).
- Keep a **held-out** portion to avoid overfitting prompts to the set.
- Version the dataset alongside prompts.
- Volume beats perfection: many automatically graded cases usually beat a few hand-graded ones.

sections.heading: Choosing graders
sections.body:
- **Code-based grading** — exact match, regex, JSON schema validation, numeric tolerance, unit tests. Fast, cheap, deterministic: use whenever an objective answer exists.
- **LLM-as-judge** — a model grades against a clear rubric (groundedness, tone, completeness). Scales to subjective criteria; must be **calibrated against human labels**, use specific rubrics, and ideally a different prompt/instance than the generator. Ask for reasoning then a discrete score.
- **Human grading** — gold standard for nuanced or high-stakes judgment; slow and costly — use for calibration, spot checks and final sign-off.

Mature programs combine all three.

keyPoints: Specific, measurable success criteria before building.
Eval sets from realistic data + edge cases + past incidents.
Code graders where possible; calibrated LLM judges for subjective criteria; humans for calibration.
Keep a held-out set; version everything.

gotchas.trap: Using LLM-as-judge to check whether output is valid JSON.
gotchas.correct: Code-based schema validation — deterministic and free.

gotchas.trap: Trusting an LLM judge's scores without checking them against humans.
gotchas.correct: Calibrate the judge on a human-labelled sample; measure agreement.

lessons.lab: Write success criteria for a support-reply assistant across accuracy, groundedness, tone and latency. For each, pick a grader type and justify it.

lessons.title: Regression testing, A/B tests and failure diagnosis
lessons.summary: Treat prompts, models and tools as versioned code with CI gates. Diagnose failures by type before changing anything.

sections.heading: Regression suites and CI
sections.body: Every change — prompt edit, model version, tool schema, retrieval config — runs the eval suite in CI. Gate deploys on thresholds per metric, and watch for **regressions on previously-passing cases**, not just the average. LLM outputs are non-deterministic, so run enough samples to distinguish real change from noise.

sections.heading: A/B testing in production
sections.body:
Offline evals predict; online experiments confirm. Run A/B (or canary) tests with:

- A **pre-registered primary metric** (resolution rate, CSAT, escalation rate) and guardrail metrics (safety incidents, latency, cost).
- Adequate **sample size** and duration for significance.
- Random assignment at the user or session level.
- A rollback plan.

Shadow mode (new version runs silently, outputs compared) is useful for high-risk changes.

sections.heading: Diagnosing failures
sections.body:
Classify before you fix:

- **Prompt/specification failure** — the model did what the prompt actually said, or instructions were ambiguous/conflicting. Fix: clarify instructions, add examples, restructure. Signal: consistent wrong behaviour that changes when the instruction changes.
- **Hallucination / grounding failure** — confident claims unsupported by the provided context. Often caused by **retrieval misses** (the answer wasn't in context) or permission to answer from memory. Fix: improve retrieval, require citations, allow "I don't know", add grounding checks.
- **Model mismatch** — the task exceeds the model's capability (deep reasoning on a small tier) or the model is overkill. Signal: failure persists across good prompts but disappears on a stronger tier.
- **Tool/integration failure** — wrong tool choice, bad schemas, errors swallowed, truncated outputs.
- **Context failure** — key information lost in a long context or after compaction.

Always inspect **traces** — what was retrieved, what the model saw — before blaming the model.

keyPoints: Evals in CI gate every prompt/model/tool change.
A/B tests need a primary metric, guardrail metrics and adequate samples.
Retrieval misses masquerade as hallucinations — check what was in context.
Model mismatch: fails across good prompts, fixed by a stronger tier.

gotchas.trap: Hallucinated answers → immediately switch to the largest model.
gotchas.correct: Inspect retrieved context first; usually a retrieval or grounding-instruction problem.

gotchas.trap: Shipping a prompt change because average score rose 1 point.
gotchas.correct: Check per-case regressions and noise across repeated runs.

lessons.lab: Take 10 failed traces from any LLM app. Label each: prompt, grounding/retrieval, model mismatch, tool, or context. Propose one fix per category.

lessons.title: Cost, latency and token optimisation; monitoring
lessons.summary: Optimise against cost per successful task and latency SLOs using caching, batching, model routing and output control — then monitor for drift.

sections.heading: The optimisation toolbox
sections.body:
- **Prompt caching** — big savings on repeated stable prefixes.
- **Message Batches API** — asynchronous processing at roughly **half the price** of standard calls, with results returned within 24 hours. Ideal for offline/bulk workloads (nightly classification, backfills, eval runs); wrong for interactive traffic.
- **Model downshift / routing** — move tasks that pass evals on a smaller tier.
- **Output length control** — output tokens cost more than input; ask for concise formats, set sensible max tokens, avoid verbose preambles.
- **Context trimming** — retrieve fewer, better chunks; prune tool outputs; compact history.
- **Streaming** — improves perceived latency (time-to-first-token), not total cost.
- **Parallelise** independent calls; avoid unnecessary sequential chains.

sections.heading: Choosing the right lever
sections.body:
Match the lever to the bottleneck:

- Large repeated system prompt → caching.
- Bulk, non-urgent volume → Batch API.
- Simple task on a big model → downshift, validated by evals.
- Slow perceived UX → streaming, smaller model for first response, parallelism.
- High output spend → format constraints.

Always re-run evals after optimisation; a cheaper pipeline that drops quality may cost more in rework.

sections.heading: Production monitoring and drift
sections.body:
Monitor continuously:

- **Quality** — sampled LLM-judge scores, user feedback, escalation and override rates.
- **Input drift** — new topics, languages, document formats, seasonal shifts.
- **Operational** — latency percentiles, error/timeout rates, rate-limit hits, stop reasons (e.g., responses cut off by max tokens).
- **Cost** — tokens and spend per task, cache hit rate.

Feed sampled production failures back into the eval set.

keyPoints: Batch API ≈ 50% cheaper, async within 24h — offline only.
Output tokens are pricier — control length.
Match lever to bottleneck; re-run evals after optimising.
Monitor quality, drift, ops and cost; feed failures back into evals.

gotchas.trap: Using the Batch API to cut costs for a live customer chat.
gotchas.correct: Batch is for asynchronous workloads; use caching/routing for live traffic.

gotchas.trap: Streaming to reduce token costs.
gotchas.correct: Streaming improves perceived latency only.

lessons.lab: For a nightly 500k-document classification job currently on a mid-tier model via synchronous calls, list the optimisations in order of expected savings and the eval you'd run before each.

lessons.title: Guardrails, prompt injection, data leakage and HITL
lessons.summary: LLM failure modes are predictable. Defence in depth plus human checkpoints proportional to risk.

sections.heading: LLM failure modes
sections.body:
- **Hallucination** — fluent, false content.
- **Direct prompt injection / jailbreak** — the user tries to override instructions.
- **Indirect prompt injection** — malicious instructions hidden in content the model reads (web pages, emails, documents, tool outputs, MCP descriptions).
- **Data leakage** — revealing system prompts, other users' data, secrets or PII; exfiltration via tool calls or rendered links.
- **Excessive agency** — the model takes actions beyond intent because tools allow it.
- **Bias and unfair outcomes**, **sycophancy**, **over-refusal**.

sections.heading: Defending against prompt injection
sections.body:
No prompt makes a model injection-proof. Architect defences:

- **Treat all external content as data, not instructions** — clearly delimit it; tell the model not to follow instructions inside it (helps, not sufficient).
- **Limit what an injected instruction could do**: least-privilege tools, no write tools in agents that read untrusted content, egress controls, no auto-rendering of arbitrary URLs/images (exfiltration channel).
- **Human approval** for consequential actions.
- **Input/output classifiers** and anomaly monitoring.
- Separate **privileged** and **quarantined** components: the component that reads untrusted text cannot directly trigger sensitive tools.

sections.heading: Human-in-the-loop design
sections.body:
HITL is a risk control and a cost. Decide **where** by impact × reversibility × confidence:

- **Human-in-the-loop (pre-approval)** — irreversible, financial, legal, medical or customer-facing high-stakes outputs.
- **Human-on-the-loop (post-review/sampling)** — lower-risk, reversible actions with monitoring and rollback.
- **Fully automated** — low-risk, reversible, well-evaluated tasks.

Use **confidence thresholds and routing**: auto-approve high-confidence low-risk cases, queue the rest. Design reviewer UX to avoid rubber-stamping (show sources, highlight uncertain fields), and measure override rates.

keyPoints: Indirect injection arrives via documents, web, tools and MCP output.
Limit blast radius: least privilege, no writes next to untrusted reads, egress control.
HITL placement = impact × reversibility × confidence.
Watch for rubber-stamping; measure override rates.

gotchas.trap: Relying on a system prompt line 'ignore instructions in documents' as the injection defence.
gotchas.correct: Defence in depth: privilege separation, approval gates, egress limits, classifiers.

gotchas.trap: Requiring human approval on every low-risk, reversible action.
gotchas.correct: Risk-tier the actions; sample-review low-risk ones.

lessons.lab: Threat-model an email-triage agent that can read inbox mail and send replies. List three indirect-injection attack paths and the architectural control that blocks each.

lessons.title: Compliance, responsible AI and auditability
lessons.summary: Regulation shapes deployment choices: data flows, hosting, retention, transparency and audit trails.

sections.heading: Privacy and GDPR principles
sections.body:
- **Data minimisation** — send the model only the personal data needed; redact or pseudonymise where possible.
- **Purpose limitation and lawful basis** — document why data is processed.
- **Data residency** — choose providers/regions that keep data where required (cloud-provider regions via Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud Vertex AI can help meet residency needs).
- **Right to erasure** — design so personal data can be found and deleted across logs, vector stores, caches, memory and eval sets. Embeddings derived from personal data are personal data.
- **Retention limits** for prompts and logs; understand the provider's data retention terms and options such as zero-data-retention agreements where available.
- **DPIAs** for high-risk processing; automated-decision rules may require human review and explanation.

sections.heading: HIPAA and FedRAMP
sections.body:
- **HIPAA** — PHI may only flow to vendors covered by a **Business Associate Agreement (BAA)** for the specific services used. Confirm which features/endpoints are covered, apply minimum-necessary access, encrypt, log access and keep PHI out of non-covered tooling (analytics, logging, chat tools).
- **FedRAMP / government** — US federal workloads typically require FedRAMP-authorized environments; Claude is available through government cloud regions of major cloud providers (e.g., AWS GovCloud via Bedrock). Verify current authorisation levels before committing.

The exam pattern: **compliance decides the hosting path and data flow first**, then you design within it.

sections.heading: Responsible AI and audit
sections.body:
- **Bias and fairness** — test outcomes across demographic slices for decisions affecting people (lending, hiring, triage); keep humans accountable.
- **Transparency** — tell users they're interacting with AI, show sources/citations, explain limitations.
- **Audit logs** — immutable records of inputs, outputs, model/prompt versions, tool actions, approvals and who approved — with access controls and retention aligned to policy.
- **Governance** — model/prompt change management, risk register, incident response playbook for AI failures.

keyPoints: GDPR: minimise, residency, erasure everywhere (incl. vector stores, logs).
HIPAA: BAA covering the exact services; PHI out of non-covered tools.
FedRAMP needs authorised gov-cloud paths — verify current status.
Audit logs: versions, actions, approvals, approvers.

gotchas.trap: Deleting a user's records from the CRM satisfies an erasure request.
gotchas.correct: Also purge from vector indexes, logs, caches, memory and eval datasets.

gotchas.trap: Sending PHI to a general-purpose logging SaaS for debugging LLM calls.
gotchas.correct: Redact PHI or log only to BAA-covered, access-controlled stores.

lessons.lab: Draw the data-flow diagram for a clinical summarisation assistant. Mark every store where PHI lands, which agreement covers it, its retention period, and how an erasure request is fulfilled.

lessons.title: Structured discovery and communicating trade-offs
lessons.summary: The architect's leverage is asking the right questions early and translating technical trade-offs into business language.

sections.heading: Structured discovery
sections.body:
Before proposing architecture, establish:

- **Problem and users** — who, what job, current process and pain.
- **Success metrics** — baseline and target; how measured.
- **Data** — sources, quality, sensitivity classification, ownership, access controls.
- **Constraints** — compliance, residency, latency, budget, existing platforms/clouds, procurement.
- **Risk appetite** — what errors cost; which actions need humans.
- **Stakeholders** — sponsor, users, security, legal, operations, data owners.
- **Integration points** — systems of record, identity provider, ticketing.

Validate with real examples: collect 20–50 representative inputs and expected outputs early; they seed the eval set.

sections.heading: Communicating trade-offs
sections.body:
Executives need decisions framed as options with consequences:

- Present **2–3 options** (e.g., fast/cheap pilot, balanced, full automation) with cost, time-to-value, quality, risk and what each requires from the business.
- Express quality as **business impact** ("about 1 in 50 summaries need clinician correction; review takes 30 seconds") rather than model jargon.
- Be explicit about **residual risk** and the controls that manage it.
- Recommend one option and say why.

Set expectations that LLM systems are **probabilistic**: quote error rates from evals, not promises of perfection.

keyPoints: Discovery: problem, metrics, data, constraints, risk, stakeholders, integrations.
Collect real examples early — they become the eval set.
Present options with business consequences and a recommendation.
Quantify error rates; never promise perfection.

gotchas.trap: Jumping to an architecture diagram in the first workshop.
gotchas.correct: Discovery and success criteria first; architecture follows constraints.

gotchas.trap: Telling the sponsor 'the model is 92% accurate' without context.
gotchas.correct: Translate into business impact and the control for the remaining 8%.

lessons.lab: Write a one-page discovery questionnaire for a new Claude use case and a three-option decision slide (cost, time, quality, risk, recommendation).

lessons.title: SLAs, feedback loops, documentation and lifecycle
lessons.summary: Production AI is a living system: define SLOs, close the feedback loop, document for handoff, and manage it through pilot, scale and retirement.

sections.heading: SLAs and SLOs
sections.body: Define service levels for **availability, latency (p95/p99), quality (e.g., groundedness rate), escalation time**. Align with what your upstream dependencies can support: model provider availability and rate limits, cloud region capacity. Design for degradation: retries with backoff, fallback models or regions, graceful "a human will follow up" paths.

sections.heading: Feedback loops
sections.body:
- Capture **explicit feedback** (thumbs, corrections) and **implicit signals** (escalation, rephrasing, abandonment, human overrides).
- Route feedback to triage: classify failures, add to eval set, fix, verify with regression run, release.
- Report a regular quality review to stakeholders with trends, incidents and actions.

sections.heading: Documentation and handoff
sections.body:
Hand off a system an operations team can actually run:

- Architecture and data-flow diagrams; threat model.
- Prompt and model version registry, with change history and rationale.
- Eval suite, thresholds and how to run it.
- Runbooks: incident response (e.g., quality drop, injection attempt, provider outage), rollback, key rotation.
- Ownership (RACI), on-call, escalation paths, cost dashboards.

sections.heading: Lifecycle
sections.body:
- **Discovery / prototype** — prove feasibility on real examples.
- **Pilot** — limited users, heavy HITL, measure against baseline.
- **Production** — SLOs, monitoring, support.
- **Scale** — more users/use cases, cost optimisation, platformisation (shared gateways, evals, guardrails).
- **Continuous improvement** — model upgrades via eval-gated migration.
- **Retire / replace** — deprecation plan when models are retired or the use case changes; migrate data, notify users.

Change management matters: train users, set expectations, involve frontline staff, and track adoption.

keyPoints: SLOs cover availability, latency, quality and escalation; design graceful degradation.
Feedback → triage → eval → fix → regression → release.
Handoff: diagrams, version registry, evals, runbooks, ownership.
Plan for model deprecation and eval-gated migrations.

gotchas.trap: Committing to a 99.99% SLA on a single model in a single region.
gotchas.correct: Align SLA with dependencies; add fallbacks and degradation paths.

gotchas.trap: Ending the engagement after launch with only a README.
gotchas.correct: Hand off runbooks, eval suite, version registry and clear ownership.

lessons.lab: Write the SLO table and incident runbook outline for a customer-facing assistant, including what happens during a provider outage.

lessons.title: Rolling out Claude Code to engineering teams
lessons.summary: Enable developers fast while keeping policy, security and cost under central control.

sections.heading: Configuration layers
sections.body:
Claude Code reads settings from several scopes. **Enterprise managed settings** (deployed by IT/admins) take the highest precedence and cannot be overridden by users; below them come command-line arguments, local project settings, shared project settings (`.claude/settings.json`, committed to the repo) and user settings (`~/.claude/settings.json`).

Use managed settings for org-wide policy: permission deny rules (e.g., reading secrets files), allowed/denied MCP servers, required hooks, model and telemetry configuration.

sections.heading: Permissions, hooks and MCP governance
sections.body:
- **Permissions** — allow/ask/deny rules for tools and commands; deny rules win. Pre-approve safe, common commands to reduce prompt fatigue; deny dangerous ones (e.g., reading `.env`, force-pushing).
- **Hooks** — user-defined commands that run at lifecycle events (e.g., before or after a tool call). A pre-tool-use hook can **block** an action deterministically — use hooks for policy that must always hold, like blocking edits to protected paths or running formatters/linters after edits.
- **MCP governance** — share approved servers via project `.mcp.json`; enforce allowlists centrally; review scopes and credentials.

sections.heading: Shared conventions with CLAUDE.md
sections.body: CLAUDE.md files give Claude persistent project memory: build/test commands, architecture notes, coding standards, gotchas. Scopes include project (committed, shared with the team), user-level (personal preferences) and organisation-level files deployed by admins. Keep them concise and specific; treat them like code (reviewed, versioned). Use custom slash commands and Skills for repeatable team workflows.

sections.heading: AI-assisted workflows and operational debugging
sections.body:
- **Headless mode** (`claude -p`) runs non-interactively for CI: automated code review, test-failure triage, issue-to-PR flows. Restrict tools and permissions in CI.
- Enforce **human review of AI-authored changes** via normal PR process and tests.
- Track adoption, cost and outcomes (cycle time, PR throughput, defect rates) — not just usage.
- **Operational debugging**: when Claude Code misbehaves across a team, check settings precedence (is a managed or project setting overriding?), the active CLAUDE.md content, MCP server status and permissions; reproduce with verbose/debug output; check proxy, auth and rate-limit configuration.

keyPoints: Managed settings > CLI > local project > shared project > user.
Deny rules win; hooks enforce must-hold policy deterministically.
Project CLAUDE.md and .mcp.json share conventions via the repo.
Headless -p for CI with restricted tools; measure outcomes not usage.

gotchas.trap: Putting 'never edit files in /infra/prod' only in CLAUDE.md.
gotchas.correct: Enforce with a deny permission rule or a blocking pre-tool-use hook; CLAUDE.md is guidance.

gotchas.trap: Asking each engineer to configure the allowed MCP servers themselves.
gotchas.correct: Distribute policy via managed settings and the project's .mcp.json.

lessons.lab: Draft a managed-settings policy for a 500-engineer org: three deny rules, two pre-approved commands, an MCP allowlist approach and one blocking hook. Then write the team's project CLAUDE.md skeleton.

flashcards.front: What are the three levels in Anthropic's agent-design guidance?
flashcards.back: Augmented LLM (single call with retrieval/tools/memory) → workflows (predefined code paths) → agents (model directs its own process). Choose the lowest that works.

flashcards.front: Workflow vs agent — the defining difference?
flashcards.back: Workflow: developer-defined control flow. Agent: model-directed control flow, looping with tools until done.

flashcards.front: When is prompt chaining the right pattern?
flashcards.back: When a task decomposes into a fixed sequence of subtasks; add programmatic gates between steps.

flashcards.front: When is routing the right pattern?
flashcards.back: Distinct input categories best handled by specialised prompts/tools/models, or to send easy traffic to cheaper models.
Sectioning (independent subtasks concurrently) and voting (same task multiple times for confidence/diversity).
Orchestrator-workers decides subtasks dynamically at run time; parallelization's subtasks are predefined.
When clear evaluation criteria exist and iterative feedback measurably improves output (e.g., translation, code meeting tests).

flashcards.front: Four conditions that justify an agent?
flashcards.back: Open-ended path, verifiable outcome/feedback, contained or recoverable errors, task value that justifies cost/latency.

Many times more tokens, coordination failures, latency, harder debugging and evaluation.

flashcards.front: Task types poorly suited to multi-agent?
flashcards.back: Tightly coupled work on shared evolving state (most single-codebase coding), latency-critical chat, low-value high-volume tasks.

flashcards.front: What goes in a good subagent brief?
flashcards.back: Objective, scope boundaries, tools allowed, expected output format, effort/budget limits.

flashcards.back: Self-review tends to rationalise its own choices; a fresh instance with separate context catches more errors.

flashcards.front: Where must business invariants (limits, authz) be enforced?
flashcards.back: In deterministic code (tools/backends), not only in prompts.

flashcards.front: Better ROI metric than cost per call?
flashcards.back: Cost per successful outcome, including retries, human review and rework.

flashcards.front: Three metric families for an AI solution?
flashcards.back: Quality (accuracy, groundedness), operational (latency, availability, cost), business (the sponsor's KPI).

flashcards.back: Thin vertical slice to real users with measurement against a baseline, then expand.

flashcards.back: Re-run the regression eval suite and stage the rollout; newer isn't automatically better on your task.

flashcards.back: Claude generalises from the reason to unseen cases; long conditional lists are brittle and dilute attention.
Diverse, representative examples covering edge cases; clearly delimited (e.g., XML tags); avoid near-duplicates the model will over-copy.
Input screening, prompt rules, tool-level controls, output screening, monitoring.
Complex multi-step reasoning, math, hard coding, planning — where evals show gains. Avoid on simple, latency-critical, high-volume paths.
More output tokens and latency; budget is configurable.
Curating which tokens the model sees at each step — retrieval, compaction, notes, subagents, trimmed tool output.
Summarising long conversation/agent history into key decisions, facts and open items to free context.
Stable → variable: tools, system prompt, large documents/examples, conversation, newest user turn.
Any change to the content before the cache breakpoint (even a timestamp or reordered tools).

flashcards.back: Unique one-off prompts, or prefixes not reused within the cache lifetime.
A folder with SKILL.md (name + description frontmatter, instructions) and optional scripts/resources.
Only name/description are preloaded; full instructions load when relevant; extra files/scripts only as needed.
Tool-selection errors, token cost on every request, larger attack surface.
Consolidate overlapping tools, task-scoped tool sets per agent/route, load on demand, remove unused tools.

flashcards.front: What makes a tool description good?
flashcards.back: What it does, when to use and not use it, parameter meanings with examples, return shape.
Structured, actionable messages the model can recover from — not stack traces, silent empties or loop-killing exceptions.
Agents and retries may repeat calls; idempotency prevents duplicate side effects (double charges, duplicate tickets).

flashcards.back: Minimum scopes, read/write separation, approvals for writes, per-user delegated credentials, secrets held by tool layer, sandboxing.

flashcards.back: Propagate end-user identity; filter retrieval by the user's ACLs before results reach the model.
OAuth 2.1-based; servers validate tokens issued for them and should not pass client tokens through to upstream APIs.
Tools (actions), resources (data/context), prompts (reusable templates).
stdio for local servers; HTTP-based (streamable HTTP) for remote servers.
MCP: reusable across many clients/vendors. Direct: app-specific tools tightly coupled to your backend, fewer moving parts.
Developer/agentic coding workflows where mature CLIs exist (git, cloud CLIs) — governed via permissions.
Trust boundaries, contracts, identity propagation, latency, observability across organisations.
Prepending short LLM-generated context about each chunk's place in its document before embedding/indexing.
Embeddings catch meaning; BM25 catches exact terms, IDs, codes, error strings. Together they reduce retrieval failures.
Rescores a wide candidate set so only the most relevant chunks enter context.
When the knowledge fits comfortably in context and is reused — use long context plus caching.
Correlation/trace ID, prompt version, model version, retrieved doc IDs, token counts (incl. cached), latency, stop reason, tool errors.
Third-party code: vet, pin versions, least privilege, allowlist; their descriptions/outputs are untrusted input.
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant; multi-dimensional (accuracy, groundedness, format, safety, latency, cost).
Realistic production-like inputs, edge and adversarial cases, past incidents; keep a held-out portion.
Whenever an objective check exists: exact match, regex, schema, numeric tolerance, unit tests.
Specific rubric, reasoning before discrete score, separate judge prompt/instance, calibrate against human labels.
Gold standard for nuanced/high-stakes judgment; used for calibration, spot checks and sign-off.

flashcards.front: What triggers a regression eval run?
flashcards.back: Any change to prompts, model version, tool schemas, retrieval config or guardrails.
Pre-registered primary metric, guardrail metrics, adequate sample, randomisation unit, rollback plan.
New version runs on live traffic silently; outputs compared offline before exposure to users.
Consistent wrong behaviour that tracks the instruction wording; fixed by clarifying instructions/examples.

flashcards.front: Common root cause of 'hallucination' in RAG?
flashcards.back: The answer wasn't retrieved into context, plus instructions that allow answering from memory.
Failure persists across well-designed prompts and disappears with a stronger tier (or the task is overkill for the tier).
About half the cost, asynchronous with results within 24 hours — for offline bulk work only.
Output tokens cost more than input and drive latency.
Perceived latency (time-to-first-token); not cost.
Input drift (topics, formats, languages), quality drift, cost drift, operational drift (latency, errors, truncation).

flashcards.front: What should happen to production failures?
flashcards.back: Triage and add them to the eval set so fixes are regression-tested.
Direct: user crafts input to override instructions. Indirect: instructions hidden in content the model reads (docs, web, email, tool output).
Limit what injected text can do: least privilege, separate untrusted-reading from privileged actions, approvals, egress controls.

flashcards.front: Data exfiltration channel to watch in chat UIs?
flashcards.back: Auto-rendered links/images or tool calls that send data to attacker-controlled URLs.
The system can take actions beyond intended scope because tools/permissions allow it.
Impact × reversibility × model confidence; pre-approve high-impact irreversible actions, sample-review low-risk ones.

Show sources, highlight uncertain fields, manageable queues, measure override/agreement rates, audit samples.
